analysis.title: US Economic Weekly: Midterms FAQs
key_insights: BofA does not expect the Nov midterms outcome to meaningfully change its economic outlook through 2028 because the scope for legislation is limited. Deficits are expected to stay near 6% of GDP, give or take a few tenths.

Baseline is a split Congress (Democrats flip the House, Republicans keep the Senate), producing gridlock with little major legislation beyond a modest defense supplemental that includes some Democratic priorities such as healthcare spending.

Republican sweep is the most consequential outcome for growth. A substantially larger defense reconciliation package than the House's Reconciliation 3.0 bill could lift growth by roughly 10-20bp in each of the next two years. The administration has requested $500bn in additional defense funding, and BofA doubts Congress approves the full amount.
A Democratic sweep differs from the baseline mainly through control over nominations to the Fed, judiciary and other posts, potentially producing more moderate nominees or leaving seats vacant.

Upside risk to the baseline: Republicans push defense spending through reconciliation in the lame duck session. BofA rates this risk low because of a crowded agenda (permitting reform, appropriations, leadership elections) and because Senate Republicans did not coalesce around Reconciliation 3.0.

AI regulation is a downside risk under unified Democratic control. BofA assumes most significant measures would face a presidential veto, but bipartisan support for some restrictions is possible given rising voter concerns. State and local rules on zoning, land use and permitting are the more important constraint, likely to slow data center construction at the margin and raise costs rather than derail the investment cycle.

After the midterms the administration is expected to pivot toward foreign policy, trade and deregulation, where executive authority matters more. Policy uncertainty could rise, but BofA expects any increase to be much smaller than the spike after Liberation Day. A more aggressive deregulatory push is expected in finance and power.

Fed call changed: BofA still expects two more hikes but now at a quarterly pace, in Dec 2026 and Mar 2027. Terminal rate forecast remains 4.25-4.5%, held through end-2027. The main risk is that moving slower lets the Fed fall behind the curve, so 25-50bp of additional hikes relative to base case cannot be ruled out.
Alternative Fed scenario: y/y core PCE rolls off on favorable base effects early next year and the Fed stops after one more hike in Dec 2026.

Oct jobs preview (Fri Nov 6): BofA expects payrolls +75k (private +70k), above the 65k consensus and up from 29k in Sep. Unemployment rate expected flat at 4.2%, with a larger participation drop able to push it to 4.1%. Risks to the downside come from slower weekly ADP and potentially unfavorable seasonals.

3Q GDP advance printed 3.4% q/q saar, above the 3.2% consensus and close to BofA's 3.5% tracking. Final sales to private domestic purchasers rose 4.9%, consumer spending 3.8% and nonresidential investment 12.7%, led by equipment and IPP.
Sep core PCE was in line at 0.3% m/m and 3.1% y/y, headline PCE 0.5% m/m and 3.6% y/y. BofA's bottom line: the economy is robust and inflation is too high.
The FOMC held at 3.875% midpoint on Oct 28. Chair Warsh said he is unwilling and unable to call financial conditions tight and declined to prejudge meetings.

Fed speakers in recent weeks lean hawkish: Logan sees at least 50bp more needed, Waller floated 25bp every other meeting up to 75bp, Collins and Williams expect a further hike, Bowman sees no urgency.
BofA card data shows total card spending per household up 6.0% y/y in the week ending Oct 24 (4.8% ex gas), with gas spending up 25.5% y/y.

Core views: 2026 growth 2.6% 4Q/4Q and 2027 growth 2.1%. Core PCE should finish 2026 slightly above 3% and reach 2.5% in 2027. Job growth is forecast to average 70k a month in 2026 and about 60k in 2027 and 2028, with the unemployment rate at 4.1% through 2027.
Rate forecasts: 2-year Treasury 5.00% and 10-year 5.00% by Dec 2026, from spot 4.60% and 4.94%. USD/JPY forecast falls from 157.68 spot to 152 by Dec 2026 and 145 by Dec 2027.

sector_views.rationale: Federal restraint on AI is limited over the next two years. State and local data center regulation is the main constraint and is more likely to slow construction and raise costs than end the investment cycle.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Above the 3.2% consensus, driven by consumer spending and AI-related capex.

risk_factors: Fed falls behind the curve by hiking slowly, which could require 25-50bp of extra hikes
Republican sweep with a large deficit-financed defense package
Data center regulation at the state and local level, plus possible bipartisan AI restrictions under unified Democratic control
Unfavorable seasonals and slowing weekly ADP for the Oct jobs report
Higher policy uncertainty from Middle East escalation or trade pressure
Net interest expense rising as Treasury refinances debt at higher rates
Upside inflation risk to BofA's forecast
charts_described: Exhibit 2 shows average annual S&P 500 total returns from 1936-2025 by party control; Democratic president with a split Congress and Democratic president with Republican Congress rank near the top at 16%, while Republican president with Democratic Congress is lowest at 9%.
Exhibit 1 shows 2027 real GDP growth of 2.2% in the baseline and Democratic sweep and 2.3% in a Republican sweep, and 2028 growth of 1.9%, 1.9% and 2.1%.
vol_and_positioning: Gridlock would seemingly be positive for markets: Savita Subramanian's team shows S&P 500 total returns have generally been strong under split government (Exhibit 2).
A Republican sweep could trigger a risk-on market reaction, reinforcing growth through wealth effects, particularly if investors see unified Republican control as supportive of AI investment.
geopolitical: Possible US escalation of tensions in the Middle East as the administration shifts focus to foreign policy after the midterms
Increased trade pressure on partners after the midterms
Much of the current inflation overshoot is attributed to tariffs and the Iran war

tension_points.bull_case: A quarterly pace of hikes (Dec 2026 and Mar 2027) is enough with solid growth and a balanced labor market, and favorable base effects could let the Fed stop after one more hike.
tension_points.bear_case: By moving slower, the Fed could fall behind the curve and end up hiking 25-50bp more than BofA's base case.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Core PCE y/y not rolling off on base effects early next year would argue against stopping after one hike.

tension_points.bull_case: A Republican sweep could add roughly 10-20bp to growth through larger defense spending and a risk-on market reaction.
tension_points.bear_case: Limited legislation under any outcome leaves growth and the deficit largely unchanged.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A reconciliation package passed in the lame duck session would move the outlook toward the Republican sweep case.
